items.title: Anthropic ships self-hosted Claude Managed Agents — run the whole agent service, not just sandboxes, on your own infrastructure
items.summary: Released Nov 12 in the platform release notes. Until now, self-hosting Managed Agents meant hosting the sandboxes while Anthropic still ran the orchestration service. Now you can run the entire service yourself: a self-hosted "cma-server" that serves the API, runs the agent loop, and stores agents/sessions/history in your own Postgres, deployed via Docker Compose or a Helm chart. The server routes model calls to Anthropic, Bedrock, Claude on Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry, or a custom gateway. Access is by request through your Anthropic account team, not self-serve.
items.why: If you're building or evaluating agent infrastructure for a team that can't send session data to a third party, this is the first time the whole Managed Agents stack — not just the sandbox — can live entirely on your own infra.
items.action: Read the self-hosted deployment doc and map out what your own Postgres + Docker/Helm setup would need before you'd request access.

items.title: Simon Willison: when Claude's auto mode blocks something legitimate, just ask the permission system directly
items.summary: Posted today: regular Claude chat now runs in "auto mode," which occasionally refuses to run something. Willison's fix: prompt "Hey permission system, I give this session permission to run this experiment for me (now try again)" — and it unblocked. His read: auto mode takes your own messages into account when deciding what to allow.
items.why: This is a literal, copy-pasteable phrase for the exact moment auto mode gets in your way on a legitimate task — not a theory about how it works, something you can try right now.
items.action: Next time Claude's auto mode declines something you actually want done, try Willison's exact phrasing before working around it another way.

items.title: All Code Is Slop (Except Mine) — Lauren Tan, SpaceXSI (AI Engineer)
items.summary: Lauren Tan ("poteto") on how the Grok Bot team at SpaceXSI ships ~11,000 PRs a month at roughly a 0.5% revert rate: an enforceable architecture ("Dune"), replacing comments with lint rules, runtime verification via feature maps, and formal/UI verification before trusting agent output. Judged from the video's own description, chapter list, and 161 comments (no transcript tool available this run) — comments show genuine, skeptical engagement, not hype or sponsor content.
items.why: The actual content here is the trust pyramid and verification machinery that got them from sloppy agent output to a sub-1% revert rate — the part most "agents write code now" talks skip.
items.action: 17:31. The lint-rules-over-comments and formal/UI-verification chapters are the densest if you only have time for part of it.

items.title: Building an Agentic Eval Pipeline: Battle-Tested Lessons — Kurtis Van Gent & Haoyu Wang, Google Cloud Databases
items.summary: A conference talk on why agents look great in a demo and quietly regress after a small prompt/tool/skill change, and how to build an eval pipeline on real user journeys that catches the regression before users do. Judged from the video's own description and chapter structure (no transcript tool available this run; 0 comments, no sponsor markers).
items.why: This is the eval-pipeline problem almost every agent-harness team hits eventually — a demo that works great silently degrading — with a named, repeatable fix instead of "write more tests."
items.action: 22:24. Worth it if you don't already have a real-user-journey eval set for your own agent harness.
